content: Contraceptive methods include a variety of options tailored to meet the diverse needs of individuals. These methods encompass female contraceptive agents, combined oral contraceptives, intrauterine devices (IUDs), natural family planning techniques, and male sterilization procedures such as vasectomy. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed practice guidelines to ensure the safe and effective use of these methods, with the third edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use serving as a cornerstone document in this effort. The WHO emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material in its publications do not imply any opinion regarding the legal status of countries, territories, or their boundaries. Additionally, the mention of specific companies or products does not constitute endorsement over others of a similar nature. While every effort has been made to verify the accuracy of the information, the WHO distributes its materials without warranty, and the responsibility for interpretation and use lies with the reader. The development of the third edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use involved extensive consultations and contributions from the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the Evidence Secretariat, and external peer reviewers. These experts participated in multiple consultations to finalize the recommendations, ensuring they are evidence-based and consensus-driven. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of these individuals and organizations, as well as the financial support provided by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). The document provides detailed guidance on the safe and effective use of various contraceptive methods, including copper-bearing IUDs (Cu-IUDs), levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs), implants containing levonorgestrel (LNG) or etonogestrel (ETG), depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) administered intramuscularly or subcutaneously, norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN), progestogen-only pills (POPs), low-dose combined oral contraceptives (COCs), combined contraceptive transdermal patches, combined vaginal rings (CVRs), combined injectable contraceptives (CICs), emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), and the Cu-IUD for emergency contraception. It also includes fertility awareness-based methods like the Standard Days Method® (SDM) and male sterilization (vasectomy). The recommendations address key topics such as initiating and continuing contraceptive methods, overcoming barriers to safe and consistent use, and the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies. The document also highlights the importance of quality care in family planning, which includes offering a wide range of contraceptive choices, providing evidence-based information on effectiveness and risks, ensuring technically competent healthcare providers, respecting informed choice and confidentiality, and delivering services in accessible locations. The WHO's family planning guidance is structured around four evidence-based cornerstones: the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC), the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR), the Family Planning Global Handbook for Providers, and the Decision-Making Tool for Family Planning Clients and Providers. These tools are designed to support healthcare providers, policymakers, and program managers in delivering high-quality family planning services. The guidelines are regularly updated to incorporate new evidence and ensure they remain relevant and effective.
